claims.text: The material family targeted for improvement is face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys derived from the Fe-Co-Ni system.
The targeted property is the orbital magnetic moment.
The primary scientific challenge is an inability to decouple the orbital magnetic moment from the spin magnetic moment.
Orbital and spin moments cannot be decoupled because available theory does not explicitly account for phonon effects.
The interplay of high configurational entropy and magnetic anisotropy contributes to the difficulty of resolving the orbital moment.
A proposed theoretical framework would explicitly incorporate phonon effects and temperature-dependent entropy into magnetic-moment calculations.
Phonon effects become significant between 300 K and 900 K in the targeted Fe-Co-Ni-based fcc HEAs.
The hardness of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating is approximately stable between 300 K and 600 K.
The wear resistance of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating decreases sharply at about 900 K.
Lattice vibrations couple to electronic orbital states in the targeted alloys.
Phonon-orbital coupling is neglected in standard thermodynamic and magnetic models for HEAs.
Thermal excitation of phonons alters local atomic symmetry.
Thermal excitation of phonons alters the local electronic environment.
Phonon-induced changes in local symmetry and electronic environment modify orbital angular-momentum quenching.
Neglect of phonons causes the orbital-moment contribution to be underestimated or misattributed.
A phonon-coupled model will predict a temperature-dependent reduction in the orbital magnetic moment.
The predicted reduction in orbital moment will align with observed degradation of wear resistance and hardness above approximately 900 K.
Current models fail to explain magnetic or mechanical degradation because they omit phonon effects.
A theoretical model for CoCrFeMnNi omits explicit phonon effects, limiting the accuracy of its predicted phase-transition temperature.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to refractory HEAs because magnetic ordering is negligible in those systems.
